questions.question_text: Which of these comparisons is a rate?

options.text: $\$150$ for $6$ hours of work
$3$ red beads for every $5$ blue beads
options.why: Beads compared with beads are the same kind of quantity, so this is a ratio.

options.text: The boys and girls in a class are in the proportion $4:5$
options.why: Boys and girls are both counts of students, so the units cancel and this is a ratio.

options.text: $2$ cups of flour for every $3$ cups of milk
options.why: Both quantities are volumes measured in cups, so this is a ratio, not a rate.

questions.solution_text:
Money and time are different kinds of quantity, so the comparison keeps its units, $\frac{\$150}{6\text{ h}}$.
The other comparisons are between quantities of the same kind.
$\$150$ for $6$ hours of work is a **rate**.

questions.question_text: Which of these comparisons is a ratio?

options.text: $250$ mL of concentrate mixed with $750$ mL of water
$\$4.80$ for $3$ kg of potatoes
options.why: Money compared with mass are different kinds of quantity, so this is a rate in $\$$/kg.

options.text: $120$ litres of water flowing in $4$ minutes
options.why: Capacity compared with time is a rate, measured in L/min.

options.text: $85$ heartbeats counted in $2$ minutes
options.why: A count compared with time is a rate, measured in beats/min.

questions.solution_text:
Both quantities are volumes in millilitres, so the units cancel.
$250:750=1:3$, with no units.
The concentrate and water comparison is a **ratio**.

questions.question_text: Bananas are priced at $\$5.50$/kg. What does this mean?

options.text: Each kilogram of bananas costs $\$5.50$.
Each $\$1$ buys $5.50$ kilograms of bananas.
options.why: This reads the rate upside down; the slash means dollars for each kilogram.

options.text: Bananas cost $\$5.50$ however many kilograms are bought.
options.why: A rate gives a price for each kilogram, not one fixed total price.

options.text: Each kilogram costs $\$5.50$ more than the one before.
options.why: The rate gives the cost of every kilogram, not an increase from one kilogram to the next.

questions.solution_text:
The slash means 'for each'.
$\$5.50$/kg reads '$\$5.50$ for each kilogram'.

questions.question_text: Which units are most likely for the cost of building a new home?

options.why: Dollars per hour measures a wage; a building cost is quoted for each square metre of floor area.

options.text: $90$ people/day
options.why: People per day measures something like population growth, not a cost.
Kilometres per hour measures a speed, not a cost.

questions.solution_text:
A building cost compares money with the floor area built.
Money over area gives units of $\$$/m$^2$.

questions.question_text: A nurse writes in a chart, 'the patient's rate is $72$.' Why is this not a properly written rate?

options.text: No units are given, so it does not say $72$ of what for each what.
A rate must always be simplified so that the first quantity is $1$.
options.why: A unit rate has $1$ as the second quantity, not the first, and that is not what is missing here.

options.text: A rate must be written as a ratio, such as $72:1$.
options.why: Ratios compare quantities of the same kind; a rate is written with units, such as $72$ beats/min.

options.text: $72$ is too large a number to be used as a rate.
options.why: The size of the number does not matter; rates can take any value.

questions.solution_text:
A rate compares two different kinds of quantity, so the units are part of the rate.
Written properly it would read $72$ beats/min.

questions.question_text: A coach compares $45$ minutes of warm-up with $2$ hours of match play. Is this comparison a ratio or a rate?

options.text: A ratio, because both quantities are times and $45$ min$\,:2$ h $=3:8$.
A rate, because the two units min and h are different.
options.why: Different units are not enough; both quantities measure time, so one converts into the other and the units cancel.

options.text: A ratio, because neither quantity involves money.
options.why: Money is not the test; a rate like km/h involves no money. It is a ratio because both quantities measure time.

options.text: A rate, because $2$ hours is a much larger quantity than $45$ minutes.
options.why: Relative size does not decide it; what matters is whether the quantities are the same kind.

questions.solution_text:
Minutes and hours both measure time, so the quantities are the same kind.
$2$ h $=120$ min, so the comparison is $45:120=3:8$, with no units left.
It is a **ratio**.

questions.question_text: Which statement explains why a rate must be written with units, while a simplified ratio does not carry any?

options.text: A ratio compares quantities of the same kind, so its units cancel; a rate compares different kinds, so nothing cancels.
A ratio uses a colon, and a colon never needs units, while a slash always does.
options.why: The symbol is not the reason; what matters is whether the two quantities are the same kind.

options.text: A ratio is always made of whole numbers, and whole numbers never carry units.
options.why: Ratios can involve decimals, and whole numbers certainly can carry units, such as $5$ kg.

options.text: A rate compares more quantities than a ratio does, so it needs more labels.
options.why: Both compare exactly two quantities; the difference is whether they are the same kind.

questions.solution_text:
In a ratio the quantities are the same kind, so written in the same unit the units divide out and only numbers remain.
In a rate the quantities are different kinds, so the number alone would not say what is compared with what.
$2:3$ is complete, but $\$2$ only becomes a rate as $\$2$/kg.
